articles.title: UK defence minister favours backchannels with Russia – a diplomacy expert explains why that would be fraught with danger
paragraphs: Britain’s defence minister, Wes Streeting, has said the UK should establish “additional channels” of communication with Russia as a way to lower the “risk of miscalculation”. His comments come at a time of heightened tension between London and Moscow over the war in Ukraine.

Backchannels have a long history in diplomacy . They have been used by the UK as part of attempts to resolve its dispute with Argentina over the Falkland Islands, as well as in efforts to end the Troubles in Northern Ireland. They have also been used extensively in Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations.

The most well-known example of this occurred between 1992 and 1993 when key Israeli and Palestine Liberation Organization figures initiated a string of secret meetings that led to the Oslo Accords. I have explored this so-called Oslo Channel in my own research .
Backchannels can provide a number of benefits. First, they can act as a means of dealing with uncertainty . This includes uncertainty around the political costs of engaging in more formal diplomacy.

For example, they allow two sides to come together when they might be willing to engage in dialogue with one another but do not want to initiate contact first to avoid being seen as desperate or weak.

Backchannels can also allow different parties, such as governments or leaders of organisations, to work out what the other side’s interests and priorities are for any negotiation. And the secrecy of backchannels allows the exclusion of groups who might want to spoil such discussion.

Second, backchannels can act as a means to engage an adversary without preconditions and, crucially, without recognising their legitimacy or validating their demands. Russian officials, for example, regularly insist that European countries accept Moscow’s geopolitical and security interests as legitimate and treat Russia as a “normal” state.

And third, backchannels can be a means of relieving tensions by acting as a “safety valve” . The late Henry Kissinger used confidential backchannels to manage US relations with the Soviet Union while he was national security advisor to President Richard Nixon during the cold war.

However, diplomatic backchannels are not without risks. Backchannels, and more importantly the contents of discussions taking place within them, can be revealed. This can damage the reputations of those who launched them, as India’s experience shows.

In 1999, India and Pakistan established a backchannel to discuss deescalating the Kargil war . The channel was leaked to the Indian press by disgruntled officials in New Delhi’s foreign office who felt sidelined by the secret negotiations.
This further damaged the relationship between India’s then-prime minister, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, and his Pakistani counterpart Nawaz Sharif, which had already come under pressure due to the war.
Embarrassing UK politicians by revealing backchannels that undermine – even symbolically – British support for Ukraine is not inconceivable with Russia.

While backchannels can help reduce tensions with an adversary, research also suggests they provide a weak foundation for longer-term changes in relations. However, Streeting’s comments appear to be less about improvising the UK’s relationship with Russia and more dealing with the immediate issue of escalation.

Another risk is that leaders can use backchannels to engage in what is known as “channel shopping” . This is where an adversary looks for the alternative communication channel where they feel the most valuable concessions can be extracted.

Russia may already be involved in a form of diplomatic channel shopping through its recent engagements with different European leaders. The German and Russian foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, for example, for the first time since 2022.

Then, one month later, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare joint call with Vladimir Putin. They said the aim of the call had been to “convey messages directly” to the Russian leader “regarding future negotiations” towards peace in Ukraine.

Peter Jones, a researcher at the University of Ottawa in Canada and practitioner in unofficial diplomatic dialogue between adversaries, has provided three tests that any UK or European minister should consider when thinking about using backchannels with Russia.
First, is the backchannel being used because secrecy is helpful for allowing new ways of addressing problems to be developed, or is it merely a means of managing the differences between the states?

Second, are those engaging in backchannels accepting and planning for its result to be put under public scrutiny? And third, is the backchannel intended to allow what would not be politically possible to take place, or is it to enable what would be illegal to take place?

The flurry of European diplomatic engagement with Russia in recent weeks may spur a fear among UK officials of missing out in diplomatic terms. However, careful and cautious use of backchannels is advised.
Both the theory and history of backchannels suggest this particular diplomatic tool can be useful, but only when handled with care.

articles.title: Nigerien women lose their rights before ever reaching a courtroom
paragraphs: Nigerien women gathered at an awareness-raising session on the fight against jihadism. Screenshot via France 24's YouTube channel. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

In 2024, Niger had a population of over 27 million. However, according to the Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey (eJNS) conducted by the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) and the Ministry of Justice, more than half experienced justice problems that year.

Overall, 61 percent of the population has experienced at least one issue accessing justice. And while men are more likely to report these problems (70 percent) than women (52 percent), this does not in any way mean women suffer fewer injustices. Instead, it underscores the fact that many women either do not recognize their challenges as justice problems or do not advocate for themselves. The survey results therefore indicate that while women need justice just as much as men, they face greater obstacles in obtaining it.

Long before reaching any courtroom, women face barriers not only within their families and communities, but also in the resolution of disputes, often over land, inheritance, and child custody. This survey also shows how the outcome of a dispute can ultimately shape a woman’s income, economic security, and ability to invest in her future.

Within Niger, the gap between men and women’s rights is obvious. As 41 percent of women say they are unaware of their legal rights, women (38 percent) are more likely than men (34 percent) to drop an ongoing court case. What’s more, almost two-thirds (64 percent) of women also have no formal education, compared to 47 percent of men.

Domestic violence (DV) is the most pressing issue faced by women in Niger, far surpassing crime, neighbor conflicts, and land disputes, with 29 percent saying they have experienced some kind of intimate partner violence. Between 2022 and 2024, domestic violence jumped from the eighth most serious problem for the general population to the third. According to HiiL, this may signal a shift in attitude toward reporting such incidents .

Across different datasets, land disputes over field boundaries, inheritance, contested sales, and crop damage rank second (17 percent) behind crime (23 percent) among the most serious justice problems. In its October 2026 report, HiiL also found that land problems accounted for 23 percent of all recorded justice problems, with a severity score of 7.1.

For women in rural areas, where more than 80 percent of Nigeriens currently live, land provides food, income, and economic autonomy. However, traditional practices, family pressures, and systems where people farm land they do not own keep their access uncertain. HiiL thereby conducted a qualitative study in the Dosso and Tillabéri regions, ultimately producing a best-practice manual for justice practitioners .

Nigerien statutory law grants women the right to own, use, and inherit land. However, in practice, customary and family rules often deny them what is rightfully theirs. In some areas, once married, women are thought to belong to their husbands’ families, precluding them from inheriting land from their birth families.

In its 2025 Annual Report, HiiL shares real-life stories, such as Saouda’s, exemplifying this reality. Widow and mother of five, Saouda lost access to her late husband’s land when his relatives claimed ownership, but successfully regained it after learning about her rights through an awareness-raising campaign.

This exclusion has a direct economic impact on those women. They not only lose inherited land, but also a source of income, food security, and the ability to invest in livestock, trade, or farm improvements.

After a separation, divorce, or the death of a partner, family-made agreements often determine where the children live, who provides for them, and whether their mother can maintain a meaningful relationship with them. These decisions are often made out of court, where customary norms hold considerable sway.

In its report, HiiL highlighted this issue through Amina’s story. Detained following a custody battle over her children, Amina thought her only hope was her family. After being told she could not legally win custody after a divorce under Islam, she had no idea she had such rights.
In this region, customary rulings tend to favor male authority in family matters, with customary chiefs typically awarding custody to fathers on religious grounds.

In 2020, the General Report of the National Consultation on Justice found that women were underrepresented in the judiciary, accounting for just 39 of the 399 magistrates in late 2017. Although customary court hearings may be more welcoming for women, no women sit among the customary assessors, prompting the report to recommend their inclusion.

For almost a third of women, preserving family relations is the main reason they do not turn to courts or customary authorities. Any woman who claims her share of inheritance or custody of her children could be seen as “causing problems” or dividing her family. Consequently, testimonies gathered across the country tell stories of women fearing they will damage their families’ honor and relatives advising them to stay silent, at the expense of their rights.
Les femmes viennent souvent nous voir après avoir épuisé leurs maigres ressources. Elles sont alors coincées, incapables de poursuivre leurs quêtes de recherche de solution à leurs problèmes.
Caught in a bind and unable to pursue their search for solutions, women often come to us after exhausting their already limited resources.

Même si je préfère aller devant le juge je ne pourrai pas car je n’ai pas les moyens. Je ne suis qu’une vendeuse d’eau fraîche et de Bissap, même si je sais que je peux aller devant le juge si mon mari ne me nourrit pas, je n’ai pas de quoi supporter les aller-retours et autres frais qu’on demande à la justice.

Even though I would prefer to take my case to court, I can’t afford it. I only sell chilled water and bissap [herbal drink]. While I may be entitled to go to court if my husband didn’t support me, I couldn’t afford the round trips and other legal fees.

articles.title: Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh
paragraphs: Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh (born 14 June 1968) is a Mongolian politician who served as the country's sixth president from 2021 to 2026. He previously served as the 30th and 31st prime minister from 2017 to 2021 and was elected to the Parliament of Mongolia four times – in 2000, 2004, 2012, and 2020.

Before his premiership, Khürelsükh served in the Mongolian government as Minister for Emergency Situations from 2004 to 2006, Minister for Professional Inspection from 2006 to 2008, and two stints as deputy prime minister between 2014 and 2017. He was the secretary-general of the Mongolian People's Party from 2008 to 2012 and its chairman from 2017 to 2021.

On 19 November 2026, President Khürelsükh was relieved of his duties, two days after he announced his resignation to refute corruption allegations and "defend his reputation" on 17 November 2026. He was succeeded by Sandagiin Byambatsogt, the Chairman of the State Great Khural, as acting officeholder until a new president is elected within four months.

Khürelsükh was born to a driver's family on 14 June 1968 in Sükhbaatar district, Ulaanbaatar, as the third of five children. His father, Ukhnaa, was born in Khentii Province, prompting Khürelsükh to take up his father's birthplace as his constituency. In an interview he gave for TV25, Khürelsükh stated that his father met his mother, a native of Govi-Altai Province, while he was making wells.

Prior to his birth, his father and older sister found a small bronze axe next to a hot spring well, thus prompting the family to name the newborn Khürelsükh, which literally means "bronze axe". Khürelsükh has one older brother, one older sister, and two younger brothers, most of whom are also drivers. According to an April 2024 article in JICA magazine, Khürelsükh stated on a 2022 visit to Japan that he "fondly remembers the warm hospitality of his host family when he came to Japan for a JICA training program as a young man."
Khürelsükh's family is reportedly related to Khand, mother of revolutionary Damdin Sükhbaatar.

Khürelsükh graduated from the Secondary School No. 2 in 1985. He graduated from the University of Defense in 1989, with a major in political studies. He studied public administration at the Institute of State Administration and Management Development and Law at the National University of Mongolia, from which he graduated in 1994 and 2000, respectively.

From 1989 to 1990, Khürelsükh served as a political deputy in the 1152nd Unit of the Mongolian People's Army. He was the first Mongolian military officer to resign from duty to maintain his party membership in 1990 when the government sought to separate party membership from various (public) offices. Khürelsükh's highest rank was colonel.

Khürelsükh worked as a political officer at the Central Committee of the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party (former communist party which ruled the country from 1921 to 1990) in the early 90s, making him one of the youngest officers in the Central Committee. Khürelsükh was appointed as adviser at the MPRP parliamentary group secretariat in 1994. Having worked there until 1996, he further rose through the ranks to become the general director of the Youth Development Center of the MPRP. This stint led him to found the Mongolian Democratic Socialist Youth Federation (MDSYF), the youth wing of the party, in 1997. He held the position until 2005, which led him to be called the leader of the party's so-called "youth faction". Khürelsükh caught the public's attention in the 1990s by organizing demonstrations and hunger strikes in opposition to the political situation at the time.

In 2000, Khürelsükh ran for a member of parliament, winning and serving two consecutive terms in the State Great Khural. While serving his second term as Member of Parliament, Khürelsükh was appointed Minister of Emergency Situations in 2004–2006 and Minister of Professional Inspection in 2006–2008. In 2007, he founded the Left-wing Association of Mongolia, an NGO that supports the Mongolian People's Party. The majority of the founding members were activists in the MDSYF, who had aged out of the party's youth wing.

Khürelsükh was successful within his party, having been elected to the Governing Board of the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party for eight years starting from 2000. In 2008, he was unanimously voted the Secretary-General of the Party. Khürelsükh served as the Secretary-General until 2012, when he resigned. In 2008, Khürelsükh was briefly interrogated after being accused of using funds from the bankrupt Savings Bank of Mongolia to purchase a car for personal use. In 2012, Khürelsükh was elected Member of Parliament for a third time. He was appointed the Deputy Prime Minister of Mongolia in 2013, serving in this role for four years until he was appointed Prime Minister of Mongolia in 2017. He was awarded the United Nations Champion for Disaster Risk Reduction in 2017.

Mongolia's parliament confirmed the nomination of Khürelsükh as the 30th Prime Minister of Mongolia in October 2017. Khürelsükh succeeded Jargaltulgyn Erdenebat, who was voted out of office in September 2017 amid allegations of corruption and incompetence. During his confirmation hearing, the new prime minister stated "My cabinet ... will declare justice again," and, added, "don't come to me with illegal acts as well as my cabinet members and don't pressure us to act illegally." One of Khürelsükh's largest projects was the oil refinery plant in Dornogovi Province. The oil refinery, established with support from India, will be capable of processing 1.5 million tonnes of crude oil per year, or 30,000 barrels per day, which will be enough to cover domestic needs.

Khürelsükh has made significant contributions to Mongolia's foreign relations. In April 2018, during an official visit to China, Khürelsükh signed 11 bilateral agreements worth $450 million, including a pact for economic and technological cooperation worth 2 billion yuan ($315 million). The Prime Minister's visit to the United States of America in September 2018 elevated the cooperation levels between the two countries to an expanded comprehensive partnership. This paved the way for Mongolia and the US to become strategic partners a year later. During the historic visit, Khürelsükh met the Secretary of State Michael Pompeo to ink the $350 million Millennium Challenge Corporation Mongolia Water Compact.

articles.title: BepiColombo
paragraphs: BepiColombo is a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) which is now orbiting the planet Mercury. The mission comprises two orbiters: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), built and operated by ESA, and Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, MMO), built and operated by JAXA. Together the satellites will perform a comprehensive study of Mercury, including characterization of its magnetic field, magnetosphere, and both interior and surface structure. In 2017, the spacecraft's cost was estimated at €1.65 billion (US$1.86 billion).

BepiColombo was launched on an Ariane 5 rocket on 20 October 2018, with a Mercury orbit insertion planned for December 2025 following one flyby of the Earth, two flybys of Venus, and six flybys of Mercury.

During launch and the cruise phase to reach Mercury, the orbiters were in a stacked configuration with two additional components: the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM), which provided power and solar electric propulsion for the cruise, and the Magnetospheric Orbiter Sunshield and Interface (MOSIF), which protects Mio from the harsh solar radiation until it is deployed. In 2024, a power-related anomaly limited the thrust of the probe's solar electric propulsion system, delaying its arrival at Mercury until November 2026.

During the probe's final approach phase to Mercury, the MTM was jettisoned on 3 September 2026, and the orbit insertion procedure for the MPO+MMO (Mio) stack was conducted at Mercury using the planned weak stability capture on 21 November 2026. However, a software glitch resulted in a shorter-than-planned thruster burn. The MOSIF will be detached from MPO on 16 December 2026 after the Japanese orbiter MMO (Mio) is deployed as originally planned on 9 December 2026 (in Germany), which would be 10 December in Japan. The scientific phase of the mission is expected to begin in April 2027.
During the launch and cruise phases, these four components were joined to form the Mercury Composite Spacecraft (MCS).

The stacked spacecraft took eight years to position itself to enter Mercury orbit. During this time it used solar electric propulsion and nine gravity assists, flying past the Earth and Moon in April 2020, Venus in 2020 and 2021, and six Mercury flybys between 2021 and 2025.

Expected to arrive in Mercury orbit in November 2026, the Mio and MPO satellites will separate and observe Mercury in collaboration for one year, with a possible one-year extension. Although originally expected to enter orbit in December 2025, thruster issues discovered in September 2024 before the fourth Mercury flyby resulted in a delayed arrival of November 2026.

ESA is responsible for the overall mission, the design, development assembly and test of the propulsion and MPO modules, and the launch. The two orbiters are operated by mission controllers based in Darmstadt, Germany. The first spacecraft operations manager of BepiColombo was Elsa Montagnon, who held the position until she was promoted to mission manager by the second Mercury flyby on June 2022. Her deputy Emanuela Bordoni acted as operations manager shortly after the second Mercury flyby, and Montagnon's post was replaced by Ignacio Clerigo by 20 June 2023. ESA's Cebreros, Spain 35-metre (115 ft) ground station is the primary ground facility for communications during all mission phases.

BepiColombo is named after Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo (1920–1984), a scientist, mathematician, and engineer at the University of Padua, Italy, who proposed the interplanetary gravity assist manoeuvre used by the 1974 Mariner 10 mission, a technique often used since then by other planetary probes.

Mio, the name of the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, was selected from thousands of suggestions by the Japanese public. In Japanese, mio (澪) means a waterway, and according to JAXA, it symbolizes the research and development milestones reached thus far, and wishes for safe travel ahead. JAXA said the spacecraft will travel through the solar wind just like a ship traveling through the ocean. In Chinese and Japanese, Mercury is known as the "water star" (水星) according to wǔxíng.
Test Einstein's theory of general relativity by measuring the parameters gamma and beta of the parameterized post-Newtonian formalism with high accuracy.

Mercury is too small and hot for its gravity to retain any significant atmosphere over long periods of time, but it has a tenuous surface-bounded exosphere containing hydrogen, helium, oxygen, sodium, calcium, potassium and other trace elements. Its exosphere is not stable as atoms are continuously lost and replenished from a variety of sources. The mission will study the exosphere composition and dynamics, including generation and escape.

The orbiters are equipped with scientific instruments provided by various European countries and Japan. The mission is designed to characterize the solid and liquid iron core (3⁄4 of the planet's radius) and determine the size of each as well as to perform gravitational and magnetic field mappings. Russia provided the gamma ray and neutron spectrometer (MGNS) to test the presence of water ice in polar craters that are permanently in shadow from the Sun's rays.

The BepiColombo mission proposal was selected by ESA in 2000. A request for proposals for the science payload was issued in 2004. In 2007, Astrium (now Airbus Defence and Space) was selected as the prime contractor, and Ariane 5 chosen as the launch vehicle. The mission was approved in November 2009, after years in proposal and planning as part of the European Space Agency's Horizon 2000+ programme. The initial target launch of July 2014 was postponed several times, mostly because of delays on the development of the solar electric propulsion system. BepiColombo is the last mission of the programme to be launched.
The two orbiters were successfully launched together on 20 October 2018. The launch took place on Ariane flight VA245 from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana.

The stacked spacecraft left Earth with a hyperbolic excess velocity of 3.475 km/s (2.159 mi/s). Initially, the craft was placed in a heliocentric orbit similar to Earth's. After both the spacecraft and Earth completed one and a half orbits, it returned to Earth to perform a gravity-assist maneuver and was deflected towards Venus.
Following its Earth flyby in April 2020, BepiColombo was briefly mistaken for a near-Earth asteroid, receiving the provisional designation 2020 GL2.

Two consecutive Venus flybys reduced the perihelion near the Sun–Mercury distance with almost no need for thrust. A sequence of six Mercury flybys lowered the relative velocity to 1.76 km/s (1.09 mi/s). After the fourth Mercury flyby in 2024, the spacecraft is in an orbit similar to that of Mercury and remains in the general vicinity of the planet.

articles.title: Why Japan’s anti-hate measures fall short
paragraphs: This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.

The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series. A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day. The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people. Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.

This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society. On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan. But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators. While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s. Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.

Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans . The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.” Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

The toothless anti-discrimination laws only manage to contain explicit discriminatory actions against disabled people, Burakumin (feudal outcasts), LGBTQ+ people, and foreigners with legal status; they have not eliminated hate speech. Meanwhile, street rallies against immigrant and imported labor have surged amid stagnant local wages, inflation, and rising living costs. Though these protests are usually small in scale, they attract a large number of social media comments, with plenty of discriminatory remarks and hate speech against foreigners.

Additionally, none of the aforementioned laws has a mechanism to force internet platforms to remove harmful content ; this results in the spread of xenophobia, homophobia, hatred against social minorities, and a racist online culture.

As Japanese national politics has stalled the enactment of the Human Rights Protection Bill, some local governments have started building the legal framework from the bottom up to address local unrest targeting ethnic minorities.

Kawasaki City, which is home to a large Zainichi Korean population in Kanagawa Prefecture, was the first municipality in Japan to introduce punitive local laws to curb protests that “ injure the human dignity of others,” as described by the city’s Justice Department.

Since the national Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Awareness was passed in 2000, the city enacted its own Children’s Rights Ordinance in 2000 and Human Rights Ombudsperson Ordinance in 2001, which paved the way for the establishment of a local independent Human Rights Ombudsperson system for receiving and investigating complaints on bullying, abuse, and discrimination.

Following a surge of demonstrations calling for the exclusion of people of foreign origin around 2013, the city enacted the Ordinance for the Creation of a City that Respects Human Rights and is Free from Discrimination in December 2019, which prohibits discrimination based on race, nationality, ethnic origin, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. The ordinance also bans using loudspeakers, placards, or flyers that induce hatred against people originating from outside Japan and their descendants. Under the Ordinance, repeat offenders would have their identities publicly disclosed, and they could be fined up to JPY 500,000 (approximately USD 3,130). The city would also keep a record of hate groups and ban them from using public facilities, such as sports venues and parks.

Furthermore, the ordinance established an expert panel empowered to review hate speech and instruct online platforms to remove extreme content targeting a specific group of people and disclose the abusers’ identities.

articles.title: Rohingya genocide case
paragraphs: The Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (The Gambia v. Myanmar), commonly referred to as the Rohingya genocide case, was a case heard by the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The case was brought by the Republic of The Gambia, on behalf of 57 members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in 2019. On 19 November 2026, the ICJ found "that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar".

The Rohingya people are a Muslim Indo-Aryan ethnic minority which has faced mass persecution and ethnic cleansing in Myanmar in recent years. The persecution of the Rohingya has been described as a genocide. Successive Myanmar governments and many elected officials have considered them illegal immigrants. But the Rohingya people argue they have lived in the area for generations and that the government of Myanmar's treatment of them is unfair to the Muslims of Myanmar as a whole.

According to The Economist, regarding Aung San Suu Kyi's motivation for taking up the defendants' cause, "It is hard to escape the conclusion that she is exploiting the Rohingyas' misery to boost her party's prospects in elections due in 2020."

Aung San Suu Kyi described this conflict as an "internal armed conflict" that was triggered by Rohingya attacks on the government of Myanmar. In 2020, the judge who presided over the case, Abdulqawi Ahmed Yusuf, gave Myanmar four months to implement his rulings: Myanmar must take "all measure within its power" to prevent genocide, until further investigation could take place, and to report back in four months.

The Gambia filed an application instituting proceedings against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on 11 November 2019, accusing Myanmar's military of committing genocidal acts against the Rohingya people during clearance operations in Rakhine State. After three days of public hearings in December 2019, the Court issued a unanimous order for provisional measures on 23 January 2020. The order directed Myanmar to prevent all acts prohibited under Article II of the Genocide Convention, ensure that its military and irregular armed units did not commit or conspire to commit genocide, and preserve relevant evidence.

Analyzing the decision in the blog of the European Journal of International Law, Marko Milanovic, a professor at the University of Nottingham School of Law, called the Court's order of provisional measures "obviously a win for The Gambia, and for the Rohingya cause more generally", but also stated that the order largely only replicated existing "state obligations under the Genocide Convention", and did not include the broader measures and statements that The Gambia had requested.

Control of Myanmar's legal defense shifted after the 2021 Myanmar coup d'état, when representatives appointed by the ruling State Administration Council replaced the civilian government's legal team and submitted four preliminary objections. Myanmar argued that the Court lacked jurisdiction and that The Gambia, as a non-injured party, lacked standing to bring the dispute. On 22 July 2022, the ICJ rejected all four objections, holding that it possessed jurisdiction under Article IX of the Genocide Convention and affirming that any state party may invoke another state's obligations erga omnes.

The case then moved into the written merits phase, encompassing Myanmar's counter-memorial, The Gambia's reply, and Myanmar's rejoinder. Alongside the main parties' filings, eleven states, including Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom, invoked Article 63 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice to intervene and submit observations on the legal construction of the Genocide Convention.

Oral arguments on the merits took place in January 2026, culminating in the Court's final judgment on 19 November 2026. The ICJ found that Myanmar had breached its obligations under the Genocide Convention by committing acts of genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State. As remedies, the Court ordered Myanmar to cease ongoing violations, prosecute perpetrators, guarantee non-repetition, and provide reparations to victims.

The ICJ delivered its verdict on 19 November 2026, finding "that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine", and that Myanmar "committed acts" that violated parts of the Genocide Convention.
9 in favor, 6 opposed -- committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.
9 in favor, 6 opposed -- violated its obligation to prevent genocide committed by individuals acting alongside its security forces.
14 in favor, 1 opposed -- did not violate the Convention through direct and public incitement to genocide by private persons in northern Rakhine State.
11 in favor, 4 opposed -- violated its obligation to punish genocide and other prohibited acts under the Convention.
14 in favor, 1 opposed -- violated its obligation under Article V of the Genocide Convention to enact the necessary legislation to give effect to its provisions.
By a vote of 14 in favor and 1 opposed, the court ordered that Myanmar must cease this ongoing violation by enacting legislation giving full effect to its obligations under the Convention.

By a vote of 13 in favor and 2 opposed, the court ordered Myanmar to take immediate and effective steps to investigate everyone reasonably suspected of committing genocide or other prohibited acts during the 2017 operations, prosecute those responsible where the evidence warrants prosecution, and punish those found guilty.
By a vote of 9 in favor and 6 opposed, the court ordered that Myanmar must provide assurances and guarantees that violations of the Genocide Convention will not happen again.

By a vote of 10 in favor and 5 opposed, the court ordered that Myanmar must allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of Rohingya displaced by its wrongful actions, whether they are in Bangladesh, elsewhere abroad or displaced within Myanmar. It must also return or replace in kind all individual and collective Rohingya property lost or damaged as a result of its wrongful actions. It must also facilitate searches for disappeared Rohingya and assist in recovering, identifying and respectfully reburial of victims' bodies according to Rohingya traditions. It must also provide rehabilitation for Rohingya who suffered physical or psychological injuries. It must also ensure that Rohingya are protected against discrimination and persecution. It must also facilitate the reunification of families.
By a vote of 10 in favor and 5 opposed, the court ordered that Myanmar must compensate the Rohingya community and individual victims for damage that cannot be repaired through restitution.

articles.title: What was the first animal that ever lived on Earth?
paragraphs: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
Imagine climbing into a time machine and setting the dial for when the very first animal was alive. You would need to travel really, really far back in time.

You would blow past the dinosaurs, which showed up about 230 million years ago . Keep going and you’d pass coil-shelled ammonites that swam in the oceans starting 450 million years ago, and then trilobites, armored animals that scuttled across the seafloor more than 520 million years ago. Further still, around 558 million years ago, you would meet Dickinsonia, a tiny, flat, ribbed oval only a few millimeters thick that looks more like a squashed pancake than any animal you know.
And even Dickinsonia was almost certainly not the first animal.
We are biologists who study single-celled life called protists . How complex life such as human beings showed up in the first place is one of the major questions in our field.
Honestly, nobody can name the first animal, but there are many clues about what it was probably like.
If we asked you what an animal is, you might say something that moves, eats and reproduces. The trouble is that plenty of nonanimals do all three.
For instance, single-celled amoebae crawl, hunt and swallow their prey whole – and they are not animals at all!

Biologists define an animal as an organism made of many cells that stick together, communicate and divide up the work of growing, eating and moving. Different types of cells specialize to do different jobs, and they all work together as one organism. And when animals eat, they take in outside material instead of making their own food from sunlight the way plants do.
Notice what is not on that list: Legs. Eyes. A brain. A mouth. That matters for what comes next.

SpongeBob SquarePants is a cartoon version of a real animal, the sea sponge . Real sponges do not wear square pants; they don’t even move around. They sit anchored to the seafloor, pumping seawater through thousands of tiny holes and straining out bacteria to eat. They have no brain, no heart and no muscles .

But sponges are still animals, and scientists often think of them as the simplest ones. Part of what makes them so interesting is a type of cell they have called choanocytes . Each choanocyte has a whiplike tail ringed by tiny fingerlike projections that trap food.

Choanocytes look almost exactly like choanoflagellates, free-living, single-celled organisms that are the closest living relatives of animals . Watching a colony of choanoflagellates feed together is about as close as you can get to seeing the doorway between single-celled life and animal life.

Imagine climbing down the animal tree of life going backward in time. You can start with animals alive today, which would be the leaves of the tree. Branches join where you encounter ancestors shared by different groups. Follow them far enough, and they all meet at a common ancestor of living animals . Scientists disagree about which groups belong on each side of that deepest branching point.

Some studies put sponges alone on one side of that fork, with every other living animal group, including us, on the other. Other studies put comb jellies in that position . In that case, these shimmering, jellylike ocean swimmers would occupy one side, while sponges and all other animals would occupy the other. This is what scientists mean when they describe either group as having “branched off first.”

It is important to remember that “branched off first” does not mean “unchanged.” Sponges, comb jellies and humans have all been evolving for the same amount of time, since our shared ancestor lived. Each lineage has followed its own evolutionary path, which over time has led to the great diversity of animals we see today, such as worms, insects, crabs and primates. Today’s sponges and comb jellies may therefore look very different from that common ancestor, making it difficult to picture what the first animal looked like.
Comparative biology can take us only so far.

Fossils are another source of information, but they show just a very narrow window into the past. Fossilization turns living material into stone, a process that works far better on hard parts such as shells, teeth and bones than on soft, squishy bodies. Because early animals were probably soft and small, they were likely easily erased from the record.

Also, fossilization works better in some kinds of environments than others. For example, muddy lake bottoms can bury dead organisms, protecting their remains from rapid decay so they have time to fossilize; any remains on wave-battered shores may wash away before they can fossilize.

Another line of evidence now available to scientists is genetic information. Genes, encoded in DNA strands inside every living organism, provide an instruction manual for how to build that creature. Cells copy that DNA and pass it on – a process that’s been going on for billions of years, generation after generation.

This genetic information accumulates slight changes over time, which scientists call mutations. It is the very existence of mutations that allows evolution – how life changes over time – to happen. This process is what generated the diversity of life you see today.

By studying the structure and architecture of DNA, as well as how it gets passed along, scientists can mathematically assemble family trees that extend very deep into the past. These family trees can help scientists make surprisingly good guesses about when and where an animal first arose. A creature’s genes hint at what it could possibly do.
Biologist Iñaki Ruiz-Trillo and his colleagues use a smartphone analogy that we find particularly useful when talking about the origin of animals.
A smartphone was not invented from scratch. Cameras, telephones, computers and the internet were all invented separately first. The innovation was combining them into a single piece of equipment.

Animals may have evolved in a similar way. Genes for sticking cells together, for sending signals between cells, for sensing the environment and for switching other genes on and off were already present in our single-celled relatives. Becoming an animal meant assembling that tool kit into one cooperating body.

The first animal was probably something very small, soft and unremarkable in an ancient ocean . It probably evolved over 650 million years ago. It certainly had different kinds of cells that were stuck together, doing specialized jobs.

articles.title: Vale, Chris Dickman: Australian science grieves the loss of a giant of ecology and conservation
paragraphs: Australia has lost one of its most distinguished ecologists and conservation champions, Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman.

Chris’s achievements and legacy are vast, much like his beloved Simpson Desert that he and his research team – known as “ the ratcatchers ” – have studied for well over 30 years. He and his team would camp out under the stars, carefully trapping and monitoring the desert’s animals and plants.

Without Chris, we wouldn’t know just how important even small but ferocious predators are in structuring ecological communities . One example is the brush-tailed mulgara, which preys on and regulates numbers of other predators, including the lesser hairy-footed dunnart .
Chris touched many in both his personal and professional roles. The authors of this article each knew Chris for many years.
Chris was honoured in a celebratory forum and festschrift, a collection of written tributes, in June that was attended by about 200 people and another 140 online. He died on November 17, 2026.
Chris’s impressive career was marked by a dedication to the scientific field and service to the wider community.

He was an internationally renowned leader in wildlife conservation who studied everything from the small marsupial Antechinus to dunnarts, long-haired rats, mulgaras, quolls, sandy inland and spinifex hopping mice and the Tasmanian devil, to name but a few species.

His work shed light on the remarkable lives these animals lead as well as the challenges they face, including feral cats and foxes . Chris was among the first to draw attention to the contentious issue of dingo management by bringing experts together for a scientific forum.
With Lily van Eeden, Chris also led a team of researchers who first estimated three billion animals had been affected by Australia’s 2019-20 bushfire crisis, garnering global attention.
What follows are our personal reflections about Chris. We hope they help convey who he was, both as a person and a professional.

Chris was a true intellect, polymath and gentleman of science. He welcomed me to the University of Sydney in 1995 and led by example in all aspects of academic life. It would be hard to find a better role model.

Over several decades we shared a commitment to discovering the ecological secrets of the red sand country of the Simpson Desert. We faced adversity in the field through floods, fires and flies, but would always smile and keep working.

I will miss the hilarious stories we shared around campfires with the many wonderful students and volunteers that joined our research efforts. Together, we would dig and delight in the way the desert came to life, particularly after big flooding rains. I will miss Chris’s writing, which was both edifying and entertaining. I will remember him when listening to the Simon and Garfunkel song, The Sounds of Silence.
It was 1998 and I was a young second-year zoology student. We had just finished a lecture that sounded like an in-person BBC wildlife documentary. The lecturer was Chris Dickman.
Soon after, Chris encouraged us students to join the Royal Zoological Society of New South Wales and I promptly signed up. Little did I know that moment would change my life.

His enthusiastic, kind and generous nature has supported many a student, colleague and friend. His door was always open, regardless of how busy he was. Chris’ passion for the Simpson Desert was contagious and persuaded many people, including myself, to make a trip to the desert year after year. Chris led by example, creating a supportive and caring environment that has ultimately shaped how I lead my own research and teaching programs.
Chris was a true gentleman scientist, mentor and friend. I will miss him greatly.

As a young PhD student, I attended the 2003 annual scientific meeting of the Australian Mammal Society in Sydney. At the time, Chris Dickman was president of the society. I was instantly struck by a few of his qualities, which in the years since have greatly shaped my own career.

Chris and his team were diligently uncovering the dynamics of the mighty Simpson Desert. Their work underscored the importance of long-term, systematic monitoring of wildlife to documenting the complex lives of mulgaras, dunnarts, native rodents and other sand-dwelling denizens. This is no mean feat, especially in an environment as unpredictable and ever-changing as the Simpson.
Chris was also a master communicator. He spoke with such clarity and with his distinctly dulcet tone, both qualities that gave his science such impact.

Most notably, Chris was incredibly generous with his time. He would ask me about my research and was always genuinely interested in what I had to say. He made young scientists like myself feel like we belonged, particularly in academia where imposter syndrome is rife. His mentorship and kind, thoughtful and supportive nature has helped me and many others pursue careers in ecology and conservation. For this, we are all forever grateful.
I was so lucky to have Chris as a lecturer during my undergraduate studies at The University of Sydney.

I fondly remember my first field trip with Chris, which involved sampling small mammals in the ancient forests of Barrington Tops in New South Wales, also known as Dungog. My peers and I slid around in the mud, attempting to reach the sampling sites, and learnt about the history of the area and its inhabitants. These early experiences shaped me as an ecologist.

I also had the privilege of working with Chris as a masters and then PhD student. I would approach him with so many ideas, some better than others. Chris always listened but, in his own style, would gently guide me in the right direction and towards fascinating topics. In our time together, we asked and answered questions about dingoes in the Tanami, foxes and cats in the Simpson, wolves in the United States and scavengers in Australia.
I owe Chris so much for his time and support. And I will forever treasure the memories of our adventures, alongside an appreciation for his knowledge and kindness.
Vale, Chris, our dear friend, mentor and colleague.
The scientist with the stellar moustache was listening, and learning, with patience, skill and grace.

Euan Ritchie receives funding from the Australian Research Council, the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action and Natural Hazards Research Australia. Euan is a Councillor with the Biodiversity Council and a member of the Ecological Society of Australia and the Australian Mammal Society. He is President and Fellow of the Australian Mammal Society.

articles.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
paragraphs: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision.
Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027.

Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight.

“As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!”

Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable.

Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.

NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website .

The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Future Engineers administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

articles.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
paragraphs: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

The same type of species, Cladosporium sphaerospermum, has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.

I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early in my Ph.D. research when I read a 2019 study from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.

Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties.

Scientists think allomelanin is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers.

Allomelanin has another remarkable property. My colleagues showed in 2021 that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity.

These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, including toxic ones, a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from natural fungi or whether it is synthesized in our lab.
In a recent study published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?

Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called organophosphorus compounds . They block an enzyme the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.

Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.

Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A 2026 analysis estimated that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.

Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well.

Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.

To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters made of a metal called zirconium . Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.

Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of metal-organic frameworks, which are among the most studied materials for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.
We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land.

For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.

Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.
This reaction usually needs alkaline conditions, which have a high pH and are the opposite of acidic – for example, baking soda dissolved in water is alkaline.

Water alone breaks down the trapped molecules far too slowly, over weeks or months. Alkaline conditions supply hydroxide, a negatively charged relative of water that is drawn to the molecule’s most dangerous bond and helps the zirconium snap it in minutes. In the lab, that means we add a liquid chemical to make the conditions alkaline, but doing so isn’t practical for a soldier’s jacket or a farmworker’s mask. Instead, we attached alkaline chemical groups directly to the particle surfaces.

We then took advantage of another property of melanin: It absorbs light and turns it into heat. Under a bright lamp for five minutes, the particles broke down about 10 times more of the stand-in chemical than they did in the dark. Simply heating the samples in the dark had a much smaller effect, which suggests light does more than warm the particles.

articles.title: 1976 Çaldıran–Muradiye earthquake
paragraphs: The 1976 Çaldıran–Muradiye earthquake occurred at 14:22 local time (12:22 UTC) on 24 November. The epicenter was located near Çaldıran, 20 km northeast of Muradiye, in the Van Province of eastern Turkey. The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.3 with a maximum intensity of X (Extreme) on the Mercalli intensity scale. The area of severe damage, where over 80% of the buildings were destroyed, covered an area of 2,000 square kilometres. There were between 4,000 and 5,000 casualties.

The easternmost part of Turkey lies within the complex zone of continuing continental collision between the Arabian plate and the Eurasian plate. The overall shortening that affects this area is accommodated partly by thrusting along the Bitlis-Zagros fold and thrust belt and partly by a mixture of sinistral strike-slip on SW-NE trending faults and dextral strike-slip on NW-SE trending faults. The earthquake was caused by movement on the Çaldıran Fault, one of the dextral faults, which had not been recognized before the earthquake. No earthquakes with magnitudes of 6 or greater were recorded within 100 km of Çaldıran in the preceding 74 years, possibly explaining why it was considered an area of only intermediate seismic risk (zone 3 out of the five-zone system of seismic risking used in Turkey at the time, with zone 1 being the highest).

The earthquake was associated with a 50–55 km zone of surface faulting, extending from three kilometres west of Sarikök in the west to just west of Baydoğan in the east. A maximum dextral offset of 3.5 m was recorded. The rupture width was estimated at 24 km and the fault zone was found to dip at 78° to the south. The duration of strong ground shaking is estimated at six seconds.

In Çaldıran, 95% of the houses were destroyed with all the others damaged to some extent, and 615 of the 3,304 inhabitants were killed. In the villages around Çaldıran, over 80% of the houses were destroyed and most of the rest were damaged; 2,313 of the 27,587 inhabitants were killed. articles.title: Readers of fanfiction have a lot in common with 18th- and 19th-century fiction lovers
paragraphs: When Archive of Our Own, the world’s largest fanfiction archive, announced that it could be unavailable for weeks following a “ security incident ”, many readers reacted with some distress . Across social media, fans half-jokingly talked about experiencing withdrawal symptoms and mourned interrupted reading schedules.
The reaction may seem uniquely digital. Yet, readers waiting for the return of Archive of Our Own have more in common with 18th- and 19th-century readers than they might realise.

Many fanfiction writers publish stories chapter by chapter, often releasing updates according to a regular schedule over weeks, months, or even years. This allows readers to follow narratives in real time. The result is a shared experience of suspense, discussion and speculation.
Long before online archives existed, popular fiction was also often consumed in instalments .

Improvements in printing technology, together with rising literacy rates and expanding commercial networks, enabled books, periodicals and newspapers to reach larger audiences than ever before . Books nevertheless remained relatively expensive commodities because of the costs associated with paper, printing and binding. One early solution was to issue works in instalments, or fascicles, which were separately published instalments of a book or other printed works. This approach allowed publishers to spread production costs, and the related financial risk, over time, reducing the upfront cost for readers. Whether by design or accident, serialisation also served to create a culture of anticipation as audiences waited for the next part of a story.

Serial publication is only part of the story. Some modern fanfiction communities are characterised by a high degree of interaction between writers and readers. Readers comment on chapters, speculate about future developments, offer feedback, and sometimes even influence the direction of a work as it is being written.

While the technologies are different, this kind of participatory reading culture would have been familiar to 18th- and 19th-century authors. Samuel Richardson, for example, encouraged and embraced interactions with readers, and was notoriously attentive to their reactions . Discussions with friends, admirers, and critics shaped his thinking about Pamela (1740); while reader response influenced the development of its sequel, Pamela in Her Exalted Condition (1741). Although increasingly dismissive of reader feedback as his career progressed, Richardson also revised later editions of Clarissa (1747 to 1748), altering aspects of the text in response to feedback from his readership.
Reading in the 18th century was also rarely a solitary activity . Books circulated through friendship networks, generated extension discussion among readers, and even performed texts aloud.

As an avid reader and frequent correspondent, many of Jane Austen’s surviving letters reveal the innate sociability of 18th-century literary culture. On February 9 1807, for example, she tells her sister Cassandra that “We are reading Clarentine, and are surprised to find how foolish it is. I remember liking it much less on a second reading than at the first and it does not bear a third at all.”

Her novel Northanger Abbey (published posthumously in 1817 but written earlier) offers a vivid depiction of this culture. The friendship between protagonist Catherine Morland and Isabella Thorpe is cemented through their shared enthusiasm for gothic novels, particularly the works of Ann Radcliffe. Chapter six sees the two girls avidly discussing Radcliffe’s 1794 novel The Mysteries of Udolpho, with Catherine declaring: “I am delighted with the book! I should like to spend my whole life in reading it.”
If Richardson and Austen capture the formation of literary communities, the reaction to Sherlock Holmes’s death demonstrates the power such communities could wield.

When Arthur Conan Doyle killed off his famous detective in 1893, more than 20,000 readers of the Strand magazine, which published the stories, cancelled their subscriptions and others wrote letters urging the author to reverse his decision. Long before readers could leave comments on fanfiction chapters or express their dissatisfaction with a book’s conclusion at an author signing, literary audiences were already seeking to shape the futures of the fictional worlds they loved.
Holmes’s eventual resurrection has become one of literature’s most famous examples of readers refusing to accept an author’s final word.

Richardson also dealt with his fair share of this. Lady Bradsheigh and Lady Echlin were two readers who were so deeply invested in the fate of Clarissa’s heroine that they suggested revisions and alternative endings to Richardson that would have changed her tragic fate. Although Richardson ultimately resisted such changes.
If a writer can’t be moved to make changes then readers can write their own stories.

One of the most well known tenets of fanfiction is its revisitation, revision and expansion of existing fictional worlds. Fans write alternative endings, explore paths not taken by the original author, and create sequels, prequels and parallel narratives that expand fictional worlds beyond their canonical boundaries.

Take Ali Hazelwood’s 2021 romance novel The Love Hypothesis, which was adapted from her 2018 Star Wars fanfic Head Over Feet . Originally published on Archive of Our Own under the pen name Ever-so-reylo, the story imagined an alternate universe to the Star Wars sequel trilogy (Star Wars: The Force Awakens,2015; Star Wars: The Last Jedi, 2017 and Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, 2019) in which enemies Rey and Kylo Ren (Ben Solo) become unlikely lovers.

We can see similar engagement with existing worlds in 18th-century works too. For instance, Poems Occasion’d by Reading the Travels of Captain Lemuel Gulliver (1727) was a response to Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels (1726) most commonly attributed to Alexander Pope. There was also John Kelly’s continuation of Pamela, Pamela’s Conduct in High Life (1741) and Henry Fielding’s satiric parody Shamela (1741).

So the desire to continue stories, debate characters, recommend favourite texts, or imagine alternative endings endures. What has changed is the speed with which these responses can be shared, the size of the communities that can form around them, and the number of people able to participate. Modern fanfiction is not a break with literary culture so much as the latest manifestation of some of reading culture’s oldest habits.

articles.title: The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history
paragraphs: The sold-out crowd at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida revived its “Gator bait” cheer at its 2026 season opener.

When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”

The decision to bring back the popular cheer reversed a ban imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide reckoning over race that followed the murder of George Floyd.

Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it remained “meaningful to the Gator family .” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has not publicly identified who formally authorized its return .

The controversy surrounding this chant has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to embrace a tradition that risks making some students and alumni feel less welcome on campus .

As an environmental and cultural historian and author of “ Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.

The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “ certain exhalation ” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.
White plantation owners eagerly took up this racist theory because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.

After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to reassert white supremacy . Alongside disenfranchisement, Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism, they promoted stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans .

One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the intimidation, exclusion and violence that African Americans routinely faced during this period.

It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A bestselling photograph bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.

The epithet soon spread through newspapers, postcards, editorial cartoons, songs and films . Ostensibly humorous images of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.

Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of historical debate . But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades.

As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a 1939 newspaper account of a home game against Georgia Tech.

When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”

While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” remained a recognizable racial slur . By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a regular fixture at Florida football games .

The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. Like most Southern universities, the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, enrolling its first African American law student, George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived four years later, and the football team remained segregated until 1968 .

Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the Confederate battle flag on his players’ helmets before the Gator Bowl .

As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual “Old South” weekend that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a mock execution of Union General William T. Sherman and a secession proclamation .

When the student newspaper surveyed the campus in 1968 about whether to continue playing “Dixie” – the unofficial anthem of the Confederate States of America – at football games, 83% of students supported the practice. But the majority of Black students surveyed opposed it. “Dixie” remained a game-day staple until 1973 .

By the late 20th century, most Florida fans no longer understood “Gator bait” through the lens of Jim Crow-era racial stereotypes. Decades of use at football games had transformed the chant into a symbol of school spirit and athletic success.

No individual played a larger role in that transformation than Lawrence Wright, the hard-hitting safety who helped lead Florida to its first national championship. Wright, who is African American, did not invent the cheer, as is often claimed, but he helped elevate it to iconic status. Following Florida’s victory over rival Florida State in 1995, he famously rallied fans with the refrain, “If you ain’t a Gator, you must be Gator bait.”

When the Gators became national champions the next season, the chant became even more deeply enshrined in Florida football culture. For most fans, “Gator bait” came to symbolize pride in the university rather than anything connected to the phrase’s earlier racist history.
While most fans were unaware of it, “alligator bait” remained a documented racial slur, creating a tension between the phrase’s historical origins and its modern meaning.
