articles.title: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
paragraphs: Between 1219 and 1221, the Mongol forces under Genghis Khan invaded the lands of the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia. The campaign, which followed the annexation of the Qara Khitai Khanate, saw widespread devastation and atrocities. The invasion marked the completion of the Mongol conquest of Central Asia, and began the Mongol conquest of Persia.

Both belligerents, although large, had been formed recently: the Khwarazmian dynasty had expanded from their homeland to replace the Seljuk Empire in the late 1100s and early 1200s; nearly simultaneously, Genghis Khan had unified the Mongolic peoples and conquered the Western Xia dynasty. Although relations were initially cordial, Genghis was angered by a series of diplomatic provocations. When a senior Mongol diplomat was executed by Khwarazmshah Muhammed II, the Khan mobilized his forces, estimated to be between 90,000 and 200,000 men, and invaded. The Shah's forces were widely dispersed and probably outnumbered—realizing his disadvantage, he decided to garrison his cities individually to bog the Mongols down. However, through excellent organization and planning, the Mongols were able to isolate and conquer the Transoxianan cities of Bukhara, Samarkand, and Gurganj. Genghis and his youngest son Tolui then laid waste to Khorasan, destroying Herat, Nishapur, and Merv, three of the largest cities in the world. Meanwhile, Muhammed II was forced into flight by the forces of Mongol generals Subutai and Jebe; unable to reach any bastions of support, he died destitute on an island in the Caspian Sea. His son and heir Jalal-al Din managed to mobilize substantial forces, defeating a Mongol general at the Battle of Parwan, but these were crushed by Genghis at the Battle of the Indus a few months later.

After clearing up any remaining resistance, Genghis returned to his war against the Jin dynasty in 1223. The war was one of the bloodiest in human history, with total casualties estimated to be between two and fifteen million people. The subjugation of the Khwarazmian lands provided a base for the Mongols' later assaults on Georgia and the rest of Persia; when the empire later divided into separate khanates, the Persian lands formerly ruled by the Khwarazmids would be governed by the Ilkhanate, while the northern cities would be ruled by the Chagatai Khanate. The campaign, which saw the Mongols engage and defeat a non-sinicized state for the first time, was a pivotal moment in the growth of the Mongol Empire.

The dominant power in late twelfth-century Central Asia was the Qara Khitai, which had been founded by Yelü Dashi in the 1130s. Khwarazm and the Qarakhanids were nominally vassals of the Qara-Khitai, but in practice, due to their large population and the extent of their lands, they were allowed to operate almost autonomously.Of these two major vassals, the Qarakhanids were by far the more prestigious; they had ruled in the area for two centuries and controlled many of the richest cities in the region, such as Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent and Fergana. By comparison, Khwarazm had only one major city in Urgench, and had only come to prominence after 1150 under Il-Arslan.

However, as the Seljuk Empire slowly fractured after the death of Ahmad Sanjar in 1154, the Khwarazmids were able to take advantage of the chaos due to their geographical proximity; Il-Arslan's son Tekish captured large cities such as Nishapur and Merv in the nearby region of Khorasan, gaining enough power to declare himself a fully-fledged sovereign in 1189. Allying with the Abbasid caliph Al-Nasir, he overthrew the last Seljuk emperor, Toghrul III, in 1194, and usurped the sultanate of Hamadan. Tekish now ruled a great swathe of territory stretching from Hamadan in the west to Nishapur in the east; drawing on his newfound strength, he threatened war with the caliph, who reluctantly accepted him as Sultan of Iran and Khorasan in 1198. The rapid expansion of what was now the Khwarazmian Empire greatly destabilized the Qara-Khitai, which was nominally the overlord. In the early thirteenth century, the khanate would be destabilized further by refugees fleeing the conquests of Genghis Khan, who had begun to establish hegemony over the Mongol tribes.

Muhammad II became Khwarazmshah after his father Tekish died in 1200. Despite a troubled early start to his reign, which saw conflict with the Ghurids of Afghanistan, he followed his predecessor's expansionist policies by subjugating the Qarakhanids and taking their cities, including Bukhara. In 1211, Kuchlug, a prince of the Naimans, managed to usurp the Qara-Khitai Empire from his father-in-law Yelü Zhilugu with Muhammad's help, but alienated both his subjects and the Khwarazmshah with anti-Muslim measures. As a Mongol detachment led by Jebe hunted him down, Kuchlug fled; meanwhile, Muhammad was able to vassalize the territories of Balochistan and Makran, and to gain the allegiance of the Eldiguzids.

Following the defeat of Kuchlug, their shared enemy, relations between the Mongols and the Khwarazmids were initially strong; however, the Shah soon grew apprehensive regarding his new eastern neighbor. The chronicler Al-Nasawi attributes this change in attitude to the memory of an unintended earlier encounter with Mongol troops, whose speed and mobility frightened the Shah. It is also likely that the Shah had grown in pride — like his father, he was now embroiled in a dispute with the Abbasid caliph Al-Nasir, and even went so far as to march on Baghdad with an army, but was repulsed by a blizzard in the Zagros Mountains. Some historians have speculated that the caliph tried to ally with Genghis Khan, especially after Mongol-Khwarazmid relations deteriorated. Mongol historians are adamant that Genghis at that time had no intention of invading the Khwarazmian Empire, and was only interested in trade and even a potential alliance. They cite the fact he was already bogged down in his war against the Jin in China, and that he had to deal with the Hoi-yin Irgen (Tumed) rebellion in Siberia in 1216.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
paragraphs: NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface.

Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base, that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure.
NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.

Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable.

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations.

While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems. Proposals are due by Dec. 21.

Nuclear power will be increasingly important to NASA’s space exploration ambitions. Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months. Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective. Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments.

LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom. Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems. This technology could enable future spacecraft to travel farther and undertake deep space missions that aren’t possible using conventional propulsion.

Together, LR-1 and SR-1 Freedom are advancing nuclear power and propulsion technologies to enable a new era of space exploration. By investing in these technologies, NASA and DOE are helping secure America’s leadership in space for decades to come.

articles.title: Great white shark
paragraphs: The great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias), also known as the white shark, white pointer, or great white, is a large shark. It is closely related to the mako sharks, the porbeagle, and the salmon shark. It is a robustly built species with a grayish upperside and a white underside. The white shark is one of the largest living shark and fish species, though it is still smaller than the whale shark and basking shark. It has about three hundred triangular, serrated teeth that are continuously replaced. Its massive, fatty liver can reach over a quarter of its body weight, providing buoyancy and storing energy. The species is partially warm-blooded, an adaptation that allows it to remain active in colder waters.

White sharks inhabit tropical and temperate ocean waters around the world and can be found both near coasts and in the open ocean. Populations are most concentrated at the Pacific and Atlantic of North America and in the waters of southern Africa and Oceania. They are a highly migratory species, traveling between the coast and the open ocean and even between continents. The white shark preys on marine mammals such as seals and dolphins, as well as squid and fish, including other sharks. It also scavenges whale carcasses. Though normally an apex predator, the species is sometimes preyed on by orcas. White sharks are generally solitary, but may gather in aggregations, particularly at feeding sites. They may communicate and establish dominance hierarchies with body language. The species reproduces with pups hatching from eggs inside the female before being born live. Juvenile white sharks typically inhabit shallower water and are limited to feeding on smaller prey.

The white shark has a fearsome reputation among the public. It is featured in the 1974 novel Jaws and its 1975 film adaptation, both of which portray it as a ferocious man-eater. In reality, white sharks normally do not prey on humans, and the majority of bites are due to curiosity or possibly mistaken identity. Many attempts have been made to keep the species in captivity, but specimens either ended up dying or being released. White shark aggregations have attracted tourists who may view them from boats or from inside shark cages.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the white shark as a vulnerable species globally and critically endangered regionally in European and Mediterranean waters. Major threats have included accidental catching by commercial fisheries, recreational fishing, and entanglement in protective nets near beaches. Several governments have enacted protections for the species, including bans on catching and killing it.

The most common English names for the species include great white shark, white shark, and the Australian English variant white pointer. These names refer to its white underside, which is noticeable in dead sharks lying upside down. Colloquial use favors the name "great white shark" or simply "great white", with great perhaps emphasizing the size and power of the species. Scientists typically use "white shark" or "the white shark" as no "lesser white shark" exists for comparison, though some use 'white shark' to refer to all members of the Lamnidae.

The scientific generic name, Carcharodon, combines two Greek words. The prefix carchar- is derived from κάρχαρος (kárkharos), which means "sharp". The suffix -odon derives from ὀδών (odṓn), which translates to "tooth". The specific name carcharias is from the καρχαρίας (karkharías), the Ancient Greek word for shark. The white shark was one of the species originally described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae and assigned the scientific name Squalus carcharias, Squalus being the genus in which he placed all sharks. By the 1810s, the shark was recognized as needing to be placed in a new genus, but not until 1838 did Sir Andrew Smith coin the name Carcharodon as the new genus.

A few attempts have been made to describe and classify the white shark before Linnaeus. One of the earliest mentions of it in literature as a distinct type of animal appears in a 1553 book by Pierre Belon. In it, he illustrated and described the shark under the name Canis carcharias based on the ragged nature of its teeth and its perceived similarities with dogs. Guillaume Rondelet would give it the name Lamia (after the child-eating monster from Greek Mythology) in his 1554 book Libri de Piscibus Marinis. The book identified it as the fish that swallowed the prophet Jonah in biblical texts.

The white shark is the sole living species in the genus Carcharodon and is one of five living species of the family Lamnidae. The other four members of this family are the mako sharks, porbeagle, and salmon shark. The family belongs to the Lamniformes, the order of mackerel sharks.

The white shark first appears in the fossil record in the Pacific basin around 6–5 mya, between the late Miocene and early Pliocene. Like all sharks, the white shark's skeleton is made primarily of soft cartilage that does not preserve well. As a result, the overwhelming majority of fossils are teeth. Nevertheless, paleontologists have traced the emergence of the white shark and its immediate ancestry to a large extinct shark known as Carcharodon hastalis. This species had teeth similar to the modern white shark's, except for the cutting edges, which lacked serrations. C. hastalis occupied a similar position in the food web to modern white sharks and was probably mostly fish-eating, with some marine mammals in its diet, though its lack of serrations made it a less efficient predator of them.

Around 8–6 mya, a Pacific population of C. hastalis evolved into C. hubbelli. This divergent lineage was characterized by a gradual development of serrations over the next few million years. articles.title: What’s behind the bedazzling mania that’s taken over high school and college campuses?
paragraphs: The art of transforming everyday objects from drab to fab is having a moment.
Bedazzling is experiencing a quasi-revival, while a newer craft, diamond painting, has emerged as its shiny cousin.
Both crafts involve placing resin gems or crystals on everything from canvases and coasters to tumblers and tote bags.

Bedazzling was popularized by DIY rhinestone application kits like the Ronco Rhinestone and Stud Setter in the 1970s and the Bedazzler in the 1990s. But whereas those older bedazzling techniques involved using a large staplerlike device to push studs and rhinestones into fabric, today’s bedazzling and diamond painting usually rely on wax or putty-infused pens to pick up and place drills and crystals onto objects and canvases. Today, a single item could be adorned by more than 100,000 gems of more than 100 colors, requiring weeks or months to complete a project.

To me, these activities are not simply fueled by boredom or nostalgia. Instead, they reflect a desire to interact with material, tangible things, as opposed to digital devices. They serve as a mental wellness practice. And they show how productivity and value are not synonymous.
As a geriatric millennial, I’ve always loved – and been known for – my shiny attire and accessories.

But it wasn’t until my colleagues who enjoy pottery and sewing suggested that I begin crafting, particularly diamond painting, as a way to boost my well-being that I considered becoming the person creating the glitz.

The art form easily accommodates the responsibilities of motherhood: It’s something I can do at home, where I can get tips from people online rather than needing to attend evening or weekend classes. And then there’s the twinge of satisfaction I experience after hearing each “pop” of the pen separating from the placed drill.
In short, I’m obsessed. The best part? I have a daily routine that doesn’t involve striving for perfection.

Unlike my teaching and research, diamond painting requires no line on a curriculum vitae or score on an evaluation sheet. Crafting isn’t about quantifying my worth or the pressure of making myself more beautiful . Its appeal lies in prioritizing myself, the experience of tranquility and the opportunity to work with my hands.
My college freshmen had different reasons for picking up the art.
Many of them came to it inadvertently. While they now enjoy bedazzling to unwind and unplug, some of them told me they originally turned to the practice to decorate their high school graduation caps.

To use a trendy Gen Z term, the craft is a form of “ whimsymaxxing ” – a way to imbue playfulness and joy into everyday life. College newspapers around the U.S. report that young women on campus are gemming anything that can hold a rhinestone. My students tell of dorm rooms wallpapered with sparkle. When they open their bags in class, I watch them retrieve chargers, lip gloss cases and water bottles, all adorned with gems arranged in impossibly intricate patterns.
Much of the media coverage of these art forms frames them as either a consumer trend – sparkle crafts are now a multimillion-dollar industry – or a form of therapy or self-preservation .

But I think bedazzling and diamond painting represent far more than that. Despite the fact that much of the history of sparkle crafts is documented solely by retailers, I see these current iterations of craftwork as part of a long tradition of women using craft as a means of self-expression, connection, catharsis and resistance against social constraints.
Crafting, in fact, underpins many activist movements .

In the 19th century, women abolitionists formed sewing circles, where they decorated objects with abolitionist emblems. Later, suffrage banners used stirring colors and messages to rally support for women’s right to vote. In 1979, an art installation called “ The Dinner Party ” commemorated women’s overlooked contributions to history through a triangular table featuring 39 place settings, each with embroidered and painted decorations. More recently, the Clothesline Project conveys the collective experience of sexual violence survivors through decorated T-shirts on a clothesline.

In a world where the message to women is either that they are too much or not enough, bringing glitz and glam into public spaces demands women be seen and rejects a “ toned-down ” or “minimalist” way of moving through the world. It shows that women are prioritizing themselves and taking the time – hours for most projects – to resist consumer culture in favor of making something new.

Amid the many stresses of 21st-century womanhood – from sexual violence and unequal pay to disproportionate childcare responsibilities and unrelenting beauty standards – bedazzling and diamond painting allow women to literally add a little shimmer to their lives, one gem at a time.

Still, women’s craftwork has long occupied a complicated space between conformity and nonconformity, or collective and individual interest. While often dismissed as unimportant forms of femininity and domesticity, craftwork continues to challenge the notion that women’s labor must serve others or offer practical application.

Of course, there’s a tension between embracing femininity and resisting the expectations attached to it. At the 1968 Miss America protests, women discarded makeup, bras and other symbols of conventional beauty standards.

Yet rejecting glamour altogether overlooks its potential for empowerment, experimentation, expression, enjoyment and connection. At the 2026 Ball Without Billionaires, Amazon workers embraced glamour on their own terms, creating their own extravagant fashion show as a way to protest the Met Gala taking place just a few miles away.
The distinction between conformity and resistance lies in the purpose behind the activity and who determines it.

Bedazzling is not automatically excluded from traditional expectations of femininity, nor does every rhinestoned object constitute an act of resistance. But a meaningful difference exists between aiming to meet expectations that include looking beautiful and choosing a messy, imperfect, playful and slow process that is beautiful to those who engage in it.
In other words, shine isn’t necessarily tacky, and a desire for beauty isn’t necessarily shallow.

There’s something supremely satisfying about slow progress and adding that last gem or rhinestone. After spending so much time methodically placing individual pieces, you can step away and soak in the entirety of the work in all its glistening glory.
Labeling women as not enough or too much has led women to choose more: more color, more sparkle, more visibility, more time spent on themselves for themselves.
Plus, there’s really no such thing as too much sparkle.
Duke University undergraduates Zoe Dakin and Rowen Spitz assisted with the research and writing of this article.
